summary: Added scripts/audit-claim-risk.mjs, a bounded heuristic scanner that a worker can run against explicitly supplied changed Markdown/MDX files to surface wording matching the avoidable rework patterns from PP-RELAY-024: unsupported prevalence/consensus language, vague anonymous-authority attribution, and strong unsupported empirical-overstatement claims. It reports file:line, matched text, and risk category so a worker can check the claim against approved repository evidence; it never rewrites prose and never establishes source validity on its own. Wired as npm run audit:claim-risk (targeted files) and npm run audit:claim-risk:selftest (deterministic fixture test), both opt-in and not part of audit:all or the build. Documented in .ai-ops/README.md as an optional aid alongside the existing manual source-claim preflight, and referenced (without changing the preflight's required checks) in .ai-ops/CLAUDE_ROUTINE_PROMPT.md.

known_limitations_and_false_positive_ris: Purely lexical/regex matching on whole words (e.g. most, many, often, commonly, typically, generally, usual(ly), rare(ly), majority; modern palmists, some writers/palmists/experts/scholars, traditional readers, experts, researchers, scholars agree; proves/proven, scientifically proven/confirmed, studies show/prove/confirm, science confirms/proves, research proves/confirms, clinically proven, conclusively/definitively proves/shows). It has no understanding of context, so grounded/attributed uses of the same words (e.g. a source explicitly saying a marking is rare) will still be flagged and must be judged by a human/worker, not auto-cleared.
It cannot verify that a flagged or unflagged claim is actually traceable to approved Tier 1-3 evidence; absence of a match is not evidence of sourcing.
It only scans files explicitly passed on the command line; it does not diff against git history or discover changed files itself.

Fenced code blocks are blanked out (to keep line numbers stable) but frontmatter and inline code spans are not specially excluded, so a match inside frontmatter or inline code would still be reported.

Deliberately not run against the existing content corpus or wired into audit:all/build, per the task's opt-in scope; running it broadly against legacy articles would likely surface many pre-existing instances of these common words that were never intended to be in scope for this task.
